title: The Cheapest Route in an Acyclic Network (Costs Can Be Negative)

concept.title: In a DAG, relax the edges in topological order: this works even with negative weights
body: Dijkstra's algorithm needs non-negative weights. But if the graph has **no directed cycle**, an edge may cost less than zero (a refund, a downhill road) and the shortest path is still easy to find, with no heap. Process the nodes in a **topological order** (Kahn's algorithm): when a node `u` is processed, every edge into it has already been relaxed (all its predecessors come earlier in the order), so `dist[u]` is final, and it can be used to relax the edges out of `u`.

Each edge is relaxed once, so the time is O(n + m), faster than Dijkstra. The same loop with `>` instead of `<` gives the longest path. With cycles and negative weights one needs Bellman-Ford (a later task). Note that the destination may be unreachable: print `unreachable`. The weights are up to 10^9 in absolute value and a path has up to 20000 edges, so use 64-bit integers.

statement: A directed graph with `n` nodes and `m` weighted edges has no cycle; weights can be negative. Print the smallest total weight of a path from node 1 to node `n`, or `unreachable` if there is no such path.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has three numbers `u`, `v` and `w`: an edge that goes from the node `u` to the node `v` with the weight `w`.
constraints: The graph has no directed cycle.
There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.
hints: Compute a topological order with Kahn's algorithm.
Process the nodes in that order and relax their outgoing edges, skipping nodes that were not reached.
If the distance of node n is still infinite, print unreachable.

solution.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).
